rationale:
Evidence from iteration 6 (score 733.1, best so far). Oval (942.8) and s-bend (931.0) both finish 20/20. Forward sensors at y=0.07 with kd 1.5 improved the slalom (progress 0.58 to 0.77), and s-bend oscillation fell (0.147). Control effort on the s-bend rose to 8.8, which is acceptable for now. The slalom is still the whole gap: 0/20 finished, with 13 off-track exits and 7 timeouts. The timeouts show the robot is now too slow for the 3 s limit on the tight alternations, not only losing the line. The oval finishes in 2.03 s, so there is little speed margin.

Changes: (1) base_speed 1.0 to 1.1. This should cut the slalom timeouts and bring average speed closer to the roughly 1.5 m/s needed. The oval has time to spare, and the s-bend control effort is the main risk. (2) mass 0.8 to 0.6 kg. Yaw inertia is mass*(L^2+W^2)/12, so this lowers the inertia the steering must overcome, and lower mass also gives faster acceleration from the same motor torque. Both should let the robot follow the alternating bends at the higher speed. Sensors, kp 2.0, ki 0, kd 1.5, wheel_track 0.11, wheel_radius and last_direction line loss are unchanged, so the only changes are speed and inertia.

Expected result: slalom timeouts drop to near 0 and progress rises above 0.85, with a chance of the first slalom finishes. Oval and s-bend should stay near 1.0 finish. Hypotheses: H1, slalom timeouts come from insufficient average speed, so base_speed 1.1 fixes them. H2, lower mass reduces the off-track exits by cutting yaw lag. Risks: higher speed may bring back off-track exits on the s-bend, and if s-bend control effort goes above 9 or oscillation above 0.2, the next step is to revert base_speed to 1.0 and keep the mass change. Next measurements: slalom completion_time and progress (to check the 3 s budget), slalom ended_by counts, and s-bend max_error and control_effort (to test speed-induced overshoot).
